catalog_quote: 4. PROSODIC TYPE The prosodic type of Elamite is not clear. The fact that the final i was neutralized (reduced), cf. hupellhupibe, proves that the final syllable was not stressed. From the fact that the vowel of the second syllable in disyllabic words, expanded by suffixation, was usually lost it may be assumed that the first syllable was stressed27. ... 27 Cf. F. Grillot-Susini, JA 282/1, 1994, 15.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held Khačikjan 1998 djvu text at p. 10 sec. 4 with fn. 27, and the Ch. III fn. 41 'stress on the penultimate' aside is also there. (2) Deciding source: a 1998 100-page grammar sketch, which for Elamite is the standard reference; the held Stolper 2004 CEWAL chapter (p. 73) and the now-downloaded Grillot-Susini & Roche 1987 (pp. 11-12) give the same picture: prosody not directly recoverable from the syllabary; final syllable unstressed (final-vowel neutralization); initial stress hypothesized from syncope of second-syllable vowels. Paper 1955 (downloaded, open access) says nothing about accent. No instrumental or prosody-specific study can exist for a language extinct for two millennia, and none of the 10 Glottolog descriptive refs is more than a sketch. (3) The classification 'undetermined' with the the primary-stress rule noting the initial-stress hypothesis fait

sources.quote: 'Enfin, les nombreuses syncopes de voyelles qui se produisent à toutes les époques et qui affectent la seconde syllabe des trisyllabiques - par ex. : pah(a)si, pul(u)hu, kut(i)ka, u(l)l(i)ra, hap(u)hu, gil(i)huna, etc. - amènent à formuler l'hypothèse de l'existence de premières syllabes accentuées et de secondes syllabes atones. Ce rythme syllabique tonique-atone pourrait expliquer, dans les mots dissyllabiques, l'instabilité vocalique de la dernière syllabe.'
